claim: Approximately 3% of random aneuploid karyotypes in yeast disrupt the stable inheritance of silenced chromatin during cell proliferation.
source: In this study, we found that ~3% of random aneuploid karyotypes in yeast disrupt the stable inheritance of silenced chromatin during cell proliferation.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from screening 3418 aneuploid colonies, of which 98 exhibited silencing defects.

claim: The chromatin silencing defect phenotype is significantly correlated with gains of chromosomes III and X.
source: Karyotype analysis revealed that this phenotype was significantly correlated with gains of chromosomes III and X.
evidence: Karyotype analysis of 24 stable aneuploid strains showed enrichment of Chr III and Chr X compared to control aneuploid strains.

claim: Chromosome X disomy alone is sufficient to disrupt chromatin silencing.
source: Chromosome X disomy alone was sufficient to disrupt chromatin silencing and yeast mating-type identity as indicated by a lack of growth response to pheromone.
evidence: Segregation analysis and conditional centromere experiments demonstrated that Chr X gain alone causes HML desilencing.

claim: Chromosome X disomy disrupts yeast mating-type identity as indicated by a lack of growth response to pheromone.
source: Chromosome X disomy alone was sufficient to disrupt chromatin silencing and yeast mating-type identity as indicated by a lack of growth response to pheromone.
evidence: Pheromone sensitivity assays showed that disome X cells have reduced response to α-factor compared to wild-type haploid cells.

claim: The silencing defect in disome X is not limited to cryptic mating type loci.
source: The silencing defect was not limited to cryptic mating type loci and was associated with broad changes in histone modifications and chromatin localization of Sir2 histone deacetylase.
evidence: qPCR analysis showed derepression of multiple genomic loci including subtelomeric genes and rDNA regions in addition to HML.

claim: The silencing defect in disome X is associated with broad changes in histone modifications.
source: The silencing defect was not limited to cryptic mating type loci and was associated with broad changes in histone modifications and chromatin localization of Sir2 histone deacetylase.
evidence: ChIP-seq analysis revealed changes in H3K4me3 and H3K79me3 modifications in disome X cells compared to wild-type.

claim: The silencing defect in disome X is associated with altered chromatin localization of Sir2 histone deacetylase.
source: The silencing defect was not limited to cryptic mating type loci and was associated with broad changes in histone modifications and chromatin localization of Sir2 histone deacetylase.
evidence: ChIP analysis and microscopy showed reduced Sir2 occupancy at HM loci and more diffuse Sir2 distribution in disome X cells.

claim: The chromatin-silencing defect of disome X can be partially recapitulated by an extra copy of several genes on chromosome X.
source: The chromatin-silencing defect of disome X can be partially recapitulated by an extra copy of several genes on chromosome X.
evidence: Integration of four Chr X genes (RPL39, RPS14B, ASF1, and DPB11) into the haploid genome caused significant HML desilencing.

claim: Aneuploidy can directly cause epigenetic instability and disrupt cellular differentiation.
source: These results suggest that aneuploidy can directly cause epigenetic instability and disrupt cellular differentiation.
evidence: The study demonstrates that specific aneuploid karyotypes cause chromatin desilencing and impair mating-type specification, which are forms of cellular differentiation in yeast.

claim: Aneuploidy is found in over 90% of human solid tumors and 50% of hematopoietic malignancies.
source: Aneuploidy, an unbalanced genomic state in which the number of chromosomes deviates from a multiple of the haploid complement, is found in over 90% of human solid tumors and 50% of hematopoietic malignancies (Mitelman et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mitelman et al., 2012.

claim: Roughly 3% (98 out of 3418) of viable aneuploid spore colonies exhibited varying degrees of silencing defects.
source: Roughly 3% (98 out of 3418) of viable aneuploid spore colonies exhibited varying degrees of silencing defects.
evidence: Direct experimental count from the screen of aneuploid colonies.

claim: No silencing defects were observed in haploid meiotic progenies (n = 100) obtained through sporulation of a diploid strain carrying the HML::YFP reporter.
source: In contrast, we did not observe silencing defects in haploid meiotic progenies (n = 100) obtained through sporulation of a diploid strain carrying the HML::YFP reporter as a control (data not shown).
evidence: Control experiment examining 100 haploid colonies showed no silencing defects.

claim: Chr III and Chr X were significantly enriched as chromosomes in gained aneuploid numbers in the desilenced aneuploid strains compared with stable aneuploid strains not selected for silencing phenotype.
source: In particular, Chr III and Chr X were significantly enriched as chromosomes in gained aneuploid numbers in the desilenced aneuploid strains compared with a set of stable aneuploid strains of the same genetic background (S288c) that were isolated through triploid meiosis but not selected for silencing phenotype (Pavelka et al., 2010) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Statistical comparison of chromosome frequencies between desilenced strains and control aneuploid strains, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Whole-genome sequencing revealed an absence of coding region mutations in the four aneuploid strains that were not already present in the parental euploid strains.
source: This analysis revealed an absence of coding region mutations that were not already present in the parental euploid strains (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Whole-genome sequencing was performed on euploid and aneuploid strains and variants were analyzed.

claim: YFP expression was heterogeneous within each aneuploid population.
source: Interestingly, YFP expression was heterogeneous within each aneuploid population, and such heterogeneity was also observed in ∆sir1 strain as reported previously (Xu et al., 2006).
evidence: Microscopy observations showed varying levels of YFP expression within aneuploid cell populations, as shown in Figure 1B and 1D.

claim: Both YFP+ and YFP- subpopulations sorted from cells with 2x Chr III and 1x Chr X gain retained the expected karyotype with gain of Chr III and X.
source: To ensure the heterogeneous expression pattern of YFP+ and YFP- signals within the population was not due to the karyotypic variations, cells with 2x Chr III and 1x Chr X gain were sorted into two distinct subpopulations based on YFP fluorescent signal for further analysis, and qPCR karyotyping showed that both sub-populations retained the expected karyotype with gain of Chr III and X (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: FACS sorting followed by qPCR karyotyping confirmed stable karyotypes in both YFP+ and YFP- populations.

claim: Transitions between repression and derepression of the HML locus occur in proliferating cell lineages of aneuploid strains.
source: To determine if this heterogeneity was due to the instability of the chromatin silencing state, we performed time-lapse imaging of YFP expression over several cell divisions in aneuploid strains. We observed transitions between repression and derepression of the HML locus in proliferating cell lineages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–G), which was never observed in haploid lineages (data not shown), suggesting that these aneuploid karyotypes disrupted the stable inheritance of the silenced chromatin.
evidence: Time-lapse imaging showed switching between silenced and desilenced states in aneuploid cells but not in haploid controls.

claim: Aneuploidy causes significant derepression of several genomic loci that are normally silenced, including subtelomeric genes YFR057W, COS12, AAD15, and PAU4 and the rDNA region gene NTS1-2.
source: This analysis revealed significant derepression of several genomic loci across different chromosomes that are normally silenced (Li et al., 2006; Ellahi et al., 2015), including not only YFP at HML but also the subtelomeric genes YFR057W, COS12, AAD15, and PAU4 and the rDNA region gene NTS1-2 (Figure 1E).
evidence: qPCR analysis showed increased expression of multiple silenced genes in aneuploid strains compared to wild-type.

claim: The desilencing phenotype co-segregated with Chr X as the only gained chromosome in segregants from the aneuploid strain with gains in Chr III (2x) and X.
source: Analysis of the aneuploid segregants obtained from the aneuploid strain (III, III, X-gain) showed that the desilencing phenotype co-segregated with Chr X as the only gained chromosome (referred as disome X hereafter) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Segregation analysis of aneuploid strains treated with radicicol showed that Chr X gain alone was sufficient for desilencing.

claim: The gain of one or two extra copies of Chr III did not affect HML silencing on its own.
source: Interestingly, the gain of one or two extra copies of Chr III, which carries the HM loci, did not affect HML silencing on its own.
evidence: Segregants with Chr III gain alone showed no significant desilencing compared to haploid controls, as shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Two extra copies of Chr III did not cause transcriptional derepression of HML:YFP, subtelomeric genes, or rDNA regions.
source: Furthermore, qPCR analysis revealed that two extra copies of Chr III did not cause transcriptional derepression of HML:YFP, subtelomeric genes, or rDNA regions (Figure 2B).
evidence: qPCR analysis showed no significant difference in expression of silenced genes in Gain III, III strain compared to WT haploid.

claim: Gaining two copies of Chr III exacerbated the silencing defect of disome X.
source: However, gaining two copies of Chr III did exacerbate the silencing defect of disome X (Figure 2A).
evidence: Microscopy analysis showed that strains with both Chr III and Chr X gains had stronger desilencing than disome X alone.

claim: A segregant with extra copies of Chr I, XII, and XIII, but not Chr X, did not show a significant difference in HML silencing compared with the haploid control.
source: Conversely, a segregant from the above karyotype with extra copies of Chr I, XII, and XIII, but not Chr X, did not show a significant difference in HML silencing compared with the haploid control (Figure 2A).
evidence: Microscopy analysis of segregants showed that Chr X gain, not other chromosome gains, was responsible for desilencing.

claim: Acute gain of Chr X induced by conditional centromere inactivation is sufficient to cause HML desilencing.
source: For both the haploid and aneuploid strains that contained the Pgal1-CEN-X construct, growth in galactose resulted in a significant increase in YFP expression from HML compared with corresponding control strains, Chr X::Pgal1, in which Pgal1 was integrated into Chr X at sites distant from the consensus centromere sequences (Figure 2C).
evidence: Conditional centromere inactivation experiments showed that acute Chr X gain causes desilencing.

claim: The fluorescence of the HML::YFP reporter in the disome X/Δsir1 double mutant was significantly higher than in either disome X or ∆sir1 individually.
source: Notably, the fluorescence of the HML::YFP reporter in this double mutant was significantly higher (p<0.05) than in either disome X or ∆sir1 individually, suggesting an additive or synergistic effect between these genetic abnormalities on HML locus silencing (Figure 2D).
evidence: Microscopy analysis showed that the double mutant had higher YFP expression than either single mutant.

claim: 23 ± 1.7% of Δsir1 cells remained in G2 after α-factor treatment for 90 min.
source: FACS-based cell cycle analysis showed that, while WT haploid cells were fully arrested in the G1 phase, 23 ± 1.7% of Δsir1% and 14 ± 1.5% of disome X cells remained in G2 (Figure 3A).
evidence: FACS analysis measured DNA content after α-factor treatment.

claim: 14 ± 1.5% of disome X cells remained in G2 after α-factor treatment for 90 min.
source: FACS-based cell cycle analysis showed that, while WT haploid cells were fully arrested in the G1 phase, 23 ± 1.7% of Δsir1% and 14 ± 1.5% of disome X cells remained in G2 (Figure 3A).
evidence: FACS analysis measured DNA content after α-factor treatment.

claim: WT haploid cells were fully arrested in the G1 phase after α-factor treatment for 90 min.
source: FACS-based cell cycle analysis showed that, while WT haploid cells were fully arrested in the G1 phase, 23 ± 1.7% of Δsir1% and 14 ± 1.5% of disome X cells remained in G2 (Figure 3A).
evidence: FACS analysis showed complete G1 arrest in wild-type haploid cells after α-factor treatment.

claim: Δsir1 and disome X strains showed significant reductions in pheromone sensitivity compared with the WT haploid population.
source: We next applied filter discs saturated with α-factor to a lawn of WT haploid, Δsir1 and disome X MATa cells. The latter two strains showed significant reductions in pheromone sensitivity compared with the WT haploid population (Figure 3B).
evidence: Halo assay showed reduced zones of growth inhibition in Δsir1 and disome X strains compared to wild-type.

claim: Hypoacetylation of histone H4 at lysine 16 (H4K16) is essential for the establishment and maintenance of silencing at HM loci and subtelomeric genes.
source: Hypoacetylation of histone H4 at lysine 16 (H4K16) is essential for the establishment and maintenance of silencing at HM loci and subtelomeric genes (Katan-Khaykovich and Struhl, 2005; Osborne et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Katan-Khaykovich and Struhl, 2005 and Osborne et al., 2009.

claim: The deacetylation of H4K16 is carried out by Sir2, an NAD-dependent histone deacetylase that localizes to silenced chromatin.
source: The deacetylation of H4K16 is carried out by Sir2, an NAD-dependent histone deacetylase that localizes to silenced chromatin (Thurtle and Rine, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Thurtle and Rine, 2014.

claim: Significantly increased acetylation of H4K16 was observed across both HM loci in disome X and Δsir1 cells compared with WT haploid controls.
source: We observed significantly increased acetylation of H4K16 across both HM loci in disome X and Δsir1 cells compared with WT haploid controls (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: ChIP-qPCR analysis using anti-H4K16ac antibody showed increased acetylation at HML and HMR loci in disome X and Δsir1 strains.

claim: Significantly reduced levels of Sir2 protein were localized to both HM loci in the disome X and Δsir1 strains, compared to WT haploid control.
source: Similarly, we performed ChIP using anti-Sir2::HA antibody and found significantly reduced levels of Sir2 protein localized to both HM loci in the disome X and Δsir1 strains, compared to WT haploid control (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: ChIP-qPCR analysis using anti-Sir2::HA antibody showed reduced Sir2 occupancy at HML and HMR loci in disome X and Δsir1 strains.

claim: The defective silencing of HM loci in disome X cells may result from a reduction in chromatin-localized Sir proteins and the corresponding increased acetylation of H4K16 at these sites.
source: These results suggest that the defective silencing of HM loci in disome X cells may result from a reduction in chromatin-localized Sir proteins, such as Sir2, and the corresponding increased acetylation of H4K16 at these sites.
evidence: ChIP data showing reduced Sir2 occupancy and increased H4K16 acetylation at HM loci in disome X cells.

claim: The Sir2-mTurq signal was more diffuse in disome X compared with WT haploid cells.
source: To further understand the mechanism by which disomy X affects chromatin silencing, we examined the localization of endogenous Sir2, tagged at the genomic locus with mTurquoise (mTurq), and observed that the Sir2-mTurq signal was more diffuse in disome X compared with WT haploid cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: Microscopy analysis showed less concentrated Sir2-mTurq foci in disome X cells compared to wild-type.

claim: The coefficient of variation (CV) of Sir2-mTurq fluorescence was significantly reduced in disomy X compared with WT haploid populations.
source: The CV was significantly reduced for Sir2-mTurq fluorescence in disomy X compared with WT haploid populations (p<0.001, two-tailed t-test), particularly in the 35% of aneuploid cells that had a significantly higher (p<0.01) mean expression of YFP from the HML locus than the haploid control.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of Sir2-mTurq fluorescence distribution showed reduced CV in disome X cells.

claim: There was a significant reduction in the percentage of disomy X cells with their HML locus attached to the nuclear envelope (zone 1) compared with the WT haploid strain.
source: We observed a significant (p<0.05) reduction in the percentage of disomy X cells with their HML locus attached to the NE (zone 1) compared with the WT haploid strain.
evidence: Microscopy analysis of HML positioning relative to nuclear envelope showed reduced perinuclear localization in disome X cells.

claim: The silencing defect of the disome X strain is associated with altered chromatin positioning in the nucleus.
source: This was accompanied by a corresponding increase in the percentage of cells with HML located in the central nuclear zone (zone 3), suggesting that the silencing defect of the disome X strain is associated with altered chromatin positioning in the nucleus (Figure 5C).
evidence: Microscopy analysis showed redistribution of HML locus from nuclear periphery to central zones in disome X cells.

claim: The number of methylated genes (~60% of total S. cerevisiae genes) in the disome X and WT haploid strains was not significantly different.
source: The number of methylated genes (~60% of total S. cerevisiae genes) in the disome X and WT haploid strains was not significantly different (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: ChIP-seq analysis showed similar numbers of genes with histone methylation marks in both strains.

claim: Both strains showed an overall positive correlation between gene expression and H3K4me3 enrichment, but not H3K79me3 enrichment.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Pokholok et al., 2005; Guillemette et al., 2011; Takahashi et al., 2011), both strains showed an overall positive correlation between gene expression and H3K4me3 enrichment, but not H3K79me3 enrichment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data showed correlation between H3K4me3 and gene expression in both strains.

claim: At the genome-wide level, there was no correlation between increased enrichment of H3K4me3 modifications and increased gene expression in disome X cells compared with the haploid control.
source: At the genome-wide level, we found no correlation between an increased enrichment of H3K4me3 modifications and increased gene expression in disome X cells compared with the haploid control (Figure 6A).
evidence: Analysis of 3502 genes showed no genome-wide correlation between H3K4me3 changes and expression changes.

claim: Most of the subtelomeric genes that were expressed and modified in both strains were significantly enriched for H3K4me3 modifications and had higher expression levels in disome X cells compared with the haploid control.
source: However, most of the subtelomeric genes that were expressed and modified in both strains (Supplementary file 2) were significantly enriched (p-value=2.5 × 10−8, Fisher's exact test) for H3K4me3 modifications and had higher expression levels in disome X cells compared with the haploid control (Figure 6A).
evidence: Statistical analysis of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data showed significant enrichment of H3K4me3 and increased expression at subtelomeric genes in disome X.

claim: Three subtelomeric genes, COS12, IMD2, and YIR042C, showed significantly increased RNA expression levels and enriched H3K4me3 and H3K79me3 modifications in disome X cells compared with WT.
source: In our ChIP- and RNA- seq experiments, three subtelomeric genes, COS12, IMD2, and YIR042C, showed significantly increased RNA expression levels and enriched H3K4me3 and H3K79me3 modifications in disome X cells compared with WT (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data showed increased expression and histone methylation at these three genes in disome X.

claim: COS12 was previously identified as a target of H3K79me3-regulated silencing.
source: Notably, COS12 was previously identified as a target of H3K79me3-regulated silencing (Takahashi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Takahashi et al., 2011.

claim: On the genome-wide level, there was no correlation between transcription levels and H3K79me3 epigenetic mark in disome X cells relative to WT.
source: On the genome-wide level or in subsets of genes carrying H3K79me only in one or the other strain, however, we observed no correlation between transcription levels and this epigenetic mark in disome X cells relative to WT (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–E and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Analysis of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data showed no genome-wide correlation between H3K79me3 and gene expression changes.

claim: None of the individual Chr X genes tested significantly disrupted silencing when present as a single extra copy integrated into the haploid genome.
source: Because cells can maintain up to four copies of centromeric plasmids, we next integrated a single extra copy of each of the top ten candidate genes into a WT haploid genome, but we found that none of these individual genes significantly disrupted silencing when present at this level (data not shown).
evidence: Integration experiments showed that single extra copies of individual Chr X genes did not cause desilencing.

claim: RPL39 and RPS14B, encoding ribosomal proteins, were among those with the strongest silencing defects when expressed on a centromeric plasmid.
source: Two genes, RPL39 and RPS14B, encoding ribosomal proteins, were among those with the strongest silencing defects when expressed on a centromeric plasmid.
evidence: Screen of MOBY library identified these genes as top candidates causing silencing defects.

claim: Overexpression of a ribosomal protein-encoding gene, RPL32, impaired silencing.
source: Since previous studies showed that overexpression of a ribosomal protein-encoding gene, RPL32, impaired silencing (Singer et al., 1998), we tested the effect of combining single extra copies, via integration, of RPL39 and RPS14B together in the haploid genome; however, this combination did not alter silencing of the HML::YFP reporter (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Singer et al., 1998.

claim: Integration of RPL39 and RPS14B together in the haploid genome did not alter silencing of the HML::YFP reporter.
source: Since previous studies showed that overexpression of a ribosomal protein-encoding gene, RPL32, impaired silencing (Singer et al., 1998), we tested the effect of combining single extra copies, via integration, of RPL39 and RPS14B together in the haploid genome; however, this combination did not alter silencing of the HML::YFP reporter (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Microscopy analysis showed no significant desilencing in strains with integrated RPL39 and RPS14B.

claim: Silencing is affected by ASF1, which encodes a nucleosome assembly factor.
source: Previous studies also showed that silencing is affected by one other top candidates from our MOBY library screen ASF1, which encodes a nucleosome assembly factor (Le et al., 1997; Singer et al., 1998; Smith et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Le et al., 1997; Singer et al., 1998; Smith et al., 1999.

claim: Integration of ASF1 together with DPB11 into the haploid genome showed no effect on silencing.
source: Integration of ASF1 together with DPB11, a top hit in our screen but not previously known to affect silencing, into the haploid genome also showed no effect on silencing (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Microscopy analysis showed no significant desilencing in strains with integrated ASF1 and DPB11.

claim: When all four genes (RPL39, RPS14B, ASF1, and DPB11) were combined by integrating them into the haploid genome, significant HML desilencing was observed compared to the haploid control.
source: However, when we combined all four genes tested above (RPL39, RPS14B, ASF1, and DPB11) by integrating them into the haploid genome, significant HML desilencing was observed compared to the haploid control, although the effect was not as strong as that in disome X cells (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Microscopy analysis showed significant desilencing in strains with all four genes integrated.

claim: The disomy X-induced desilencing is complex and requires the combined effects of at least four Chr X-linked genes.
source: These results suggest that the disomy X-induced desilencing is complex and requires the combined effects of at least four Chr X-linked genes.
evidence: Integration experiments showed that four genes together, but not individually or in pairs, partially recapitulate disome X desilencing.

claim: Approximately 100% of colonies resulting from triploid meiosis are aneuploid with random combinations of chromosome numbers.
source: Previous studies showed that ~100% of the resulting colonies were aneuploid with random combinations of chromosome numbers, due to the segregation of 3 sets of homologous chromosomes during meiosis (Campbell et al., 1981; Pavelka et al., 2010; St Charles et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Campbell et al., 1981; Pavelka et al., 2010; St Charles et al., 2010.

claim: Chromatin silencing at HML and HMR is critical for the specification of the sexual identity of yeast, in the form of a or α mating type, which is stably inherited from generation to generation.
source: In particular, chromatin silencing at HML and HMR is critical for the specification of the sexual identity of yeast, in the form of a or α mating type, which is stably inherited from generation to generation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast mating-type specification.

claim: The underlying epigenetic mechanism of mating type specification depends on the recruitment of the Sir2 NAD-dependent histone deacetylase to HM loci through interactions with other Sir proteins (Sir1, 3, and 4) and several other accessory factors.
source: The underlying epigenetic mechanism of mating type specification depends on the recruitment of the Sir2 NAD-dependent histone deacetylase to HM loci through interactions with other Sir proteins (Sir1, 3, and 4) and several other accessory factors (Liou et al., 2005; Kueng et al., 2013; Behrouzi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Liou et al., 2005; Kueng et al., 2013; Behrouzi et al., 2016.

claim: Spreading of the Sir protein complex across the HM region of DNA leads to hypoacetylated histones and establishes stably silenced chromatin.
source: Spreading of the Sir protein complex across this region of DNA leads to hypoacetylated histones and establishes stably silenced chromatin (Rusche et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rusche et al., 2003.

claim: Aneuploidy is correlated with complex patterns of altered gene transcription.
source: Aneuploidy is correlated with complex patterns of altered gene transcription (Upender et al., 2004; Ried et al., 2012), but its potential impact on the epigenetic state of cancer cells remains unclear due to the co-existence of the other genetic alterations in highly complex and unstable cancer genomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Upender et al., 2004; Ried et al., 2012.

claim: Chromosome copy number variation in yeast leads to scaled changes in the transcriptome and proteome for most of the genes carried on the aneuploid chromosome.
source: In yeast, chromosome copy number variation leads to scaled changes in the transcriptome and proteome for most of the genes carried on the aneuploid chromosome, as well as expression level changes that vary significantly more than the scaled amount for 5–10% of total genes distributed throughout the genome (Torres et al., 2007; Rancati et al., 2008; Pavelka et al., 2010; Sheltzer et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Torres et al., 2007; Rancati et al., 2008; Pavelka et al., 2010; Sheltzer et al., 2012.

claim: Expression level changes vary significantly more than the scaled amount for 5–10% of total genes distributed throughout the genome in aneuploid yeast.
source: In yeast, chromosome copy number variation leads to scaled changes in the transcriptome and proteome for most of the genes carried on the aneuploid chromosome, as well as expression level changes that vary significantly more than the scaled amount for 5–10% of total genes distributed throughout the genome (Torres et al., 2007; Rancati et al., 2008; Pavelka et al., 2010; Sheltzer et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Torres et al., 2007; Rancati et al., 2008; Pavelka et al., 2010; Sheltzer et al., 2012.

claim: Yeast cells lack complex developmental fates.
source: This is in part because yeast cells lack complex developmental fates and yeast genome comprises mostly open chromatin accessible to the transcriptional machinery (Millar and Grunstein, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast biology.

claim: Yeast genome comprises mostly open chromatin accessible to the transcriptional machinery.
source: This is in part because yeast cells lack complex developmental fates and yeast genome comprises mostly open chromatin accessible to the transcriptional machinery (Millar and Grunstein, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Millar and Grunstein, 2006.

claim: Yeast cells have a few well-established regions of silenced chromatin, including the cryptic mating type loci HML and HMR on chromosome III, the rDNA repeats on chromosome XII, and subtelomeric regions.
source: Yeast cells, however, do have a few well-established regions of silenced chromatin, including the cryptic mating type loci HML and HMR on chromosome III, the rDNA repeats on chromosome XII, and subtelomeric regions (Bühler and Gasser, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bühler and Gasser, 2009.

claim: Alterations in epigenetic modifications have been recognized as a key step in the initiation and progression of cancer.
source: Alterations in epigenetic modifications have been recognized as a key step in the initiation and progression of cancer whereby quiescent or slowly-dividing somatic cells escape their normal differentiated state and undergo precocious proliferation. (Feinberg et al., 2006; Timp and Feinberg, 2013; Morgan and Shilatifard, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Feinberg et al., 2006; Timp and Feinberg, 2013; Morgan and Shilatifard, 2015.

claim: The histone modification landscape and the associated open or closed (silenced) chromatin conformations regulate access to the genetic information by the transcriptional machinery.
source: The histone modification landscape and the associated open or closed (silenced) chromatin conformations regulate access to the genetic information by the transcriptional machinery and provide a mechanism for the establishment and maintenance of stable epigenetic states in well-differentiated cells and tissues (Jaenisch and Bird, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jaenisch and Bird, 2003.

claim: The silencing of the HM loci and subtelomeric regions is associated with characteristic distributions for both Sir2 protein and the chromatin regions within the nucleus.
source: The silencing of the HM loci and subtelomeric regions is associated with characteristic distributions for both Sir2 protein and the chromatin regions within the nucleus (Andrulis et al., 1998; Taddei et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Andrulis et al., 1998; Taddei et al., 2009.

claim: The more dispersed Sir2 distribution in disome X cells is consistent with the reduced concentration of Sir2 in silenced chromatin regions.
source: The more dispersed Sir2 distribution in disome X cells is consistent with the reduced concentration of Sir2 in silenced chromatin regions (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the ChIP data showing reduced Sir2 occupancy at HM loci and microscopy showing diffuse Sir2 distribution.

claim: The positioning of chromatin relative to the nuclear envelope is important for silencing.
source: The positioning of chromatin relative to the nuclear envelope is also important for silencing (Bystricky et al., 2009; Mekhail and Moazed, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bystricky et al., 2009; Mekhail and Moazed, 2010.

claim: The silencing function of Sir2 requires its concentration to perinuclear pools.
source: The diffused Sir2 distribution, particularly in cells with desilenced HML gene expression, is consistent with previous reports that the silencing function of this protein requires its concentration to perinuclear pools (Hoppe et al., 2002; Taddei et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hoppe et al., 2002; Taddei et al., 2009.

claim: Studies of the transcriptome in trisomy 21 human fibroblasts show that the overall nuclear organization defined by lamin-associated domains (LADs) is intact in these cells.
source: Studies of the transcriptome in trisomy 21 human fibroblasts show that, although the overall nuclear organization defined by lamin-associated domains (LADs) is intact in these cells, alterations in H3K4me3 correlate with specialized gene expression dysregulation domains (GEDDs) (Letourneau et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Letourneau et al., 2014.

claim: Alterations in H3K4me3 correlate with specialized gene expression dysregulation domains (GEDDs) in trisomy 21 human fibroblasts.
source: Studies of the transcriptome in trisomy 21 human fibroblasts show that, although the overall nuclear organization defined by lamin-associated domains (LADs) is intact in these cells, alterations in H3K4me3 correlate with specialized gene expression dysregulation domains (GEDDs) (Letourneau et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Letourneau et al., 2014.

claim: A perturbed nuclear compartmentalization, which causes changes in gene expression, may be an emergent outcome of gene copy number imbalance associated with certain chromosome aneuploidy.
source: This finding together with our results suggests that a perturbed nuclear compartmentalization, which causes changes in gene expression, may be an emergent outcome of gene copy number imbalance associated with certain chromosome aneuploidy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current study's findings and the cited trisomy 21 study.

claim: Epigenetic states are acquired through a precise balance between euchromatin and heterochromatin and are an essential mechanism to control proper cellular identity.
source: Epigenetic states are acquired through a precise balance between euchromatin and heterochromatin and are an essential mechanism to control proper cellular identity (Jaenisch and Bird, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jaenisch and Bird, 2003.

claim: Numerical alterations in chromosomes can derepress heterochromatin to break the delicate balance between euchromatin and heterochromatin, relax epigenetic inheritance, and cause stochastic variation in cell identity that impairs the responsiveness to regulatory factors.
source: Here, we have shown that numerical alterations in chromosomes can derepress heterochromatin to break this delicate balance, relax epigenetic inheritance, and cause stochastic variation in cell identity that impairs the responsiveness to regulatory factors.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the experimental findings showing desilencing, heterogeneous expression, and impaired pheromone response in aneuploid cells.

claim: The aneuploidy-induced changes in heterochromatin inheritance and histone-modification landscape may be an important mechanism by which chromosomal instability drives large-scale phenotypic variability during tumor evolution.
source: The aneuploidy-induced changes in heterochromatin inheritance and histone-modification landscape may be an important mechanism by which chromosomal instability drives large-scale phenotypic variability during tumor evolution.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential implications for cancer biology.

claim: Most aneuploid yeast obtained through triploid meiosis are karyotypically unstable.
source: Using fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) and qPCR karyotyping analyses, as previously described (Pavelka et al., 2010), we identified 24 aneuploid strains with unique and stable karyotypes, each with gain or loss of multiple chromosomes compared to the basal ploidy – defined as the copy number possessed by most chromosomes (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The need to screen for stable karyotypes implies that most are unstable, as stated elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: H3K4 trimethylation is considered to be a mark of active transcription.
source: H3K4 trimethylation is considered to be a mark of active transcription, given that its occupancy is generally high at the promoters of actively transcribed genes (Pokholok et al., 2005; Guillemette et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pokholok et al., 2005; Guillemette et al., 2011.

claim: H3K4 trimethylation is carried out by the Set1 complex.
source: In yeast, H3K4 trimethylation is carried out by the Set1 complex and transcriptional outcomes related to changes in this mark are partially dependent on the location of genes in active or silent chromatin regions (Bryk et al., 2002; Krogan et al., 2002; Santos-Rosa et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bryk et al., 2002; Krogan et al., 2002; Santos-Rosa et al., 2002.

claim: H3K4 is generally hypermethylated within regions of euchromatin and hypomethylated within heterochromatin.
source: Although H3K4 is generally hypermethylated within regions of euchromatin and hypomethylated within heterochromatin, loss of H3K4me3 due to deletion of SET1 had little effect on coding gene expression (Margaritis et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Margaritis et al., 2012.

claim: Loss of H3K4me3 due to deletion of SET1 had little effect on coding gene expression.
source: Although H3K4 is generally hypermethylated within regions of euchromatin and hypomethylated within heterochromatin, loss of H3K4me3 due to deletion of SET1 had little effect on coding gene expression (Margaritis et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Margaritis et al., 2012.

claim: Both H3K4me3 modifications and gene expression were increased at subtelomeric genes in disome X cells compared with the haploid control strain.
source: However, in the case of silent domains, such as subtelomeric genes, we indeed found that both H3K4me3 modifications and gene expression were increased in disome X cells compared with the haploid control strain.
evidence: ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data showed increased H3K4me3 and expression at subtelomeric genes in disome X.

claim: Most of the subtelomeric genes are not strongly affected by Chr X disomy.
source: It should be noted, however, that RNA-seq data showed that most of the subtelomeric genes are not strongly affected by Chr X disomy, suggesting that this aneuploidy does not have a general effect on silencing at subtelomeres.
evidence: RNA-seq analysis showed that only a subset of subtelomeric genes were significantly affected.

claim: Expression of subtelomeric genes in S. cerevisiae is largely uninfluenced by mutations in Sir proteins.
source: However, this is consistent with the previous observation that expression of subtelomeric genes in S. cerevisiae is largely uninfluenced by mutations in Sir proteins and Sir-based silencing is not a widespread phenomenon at telomeres despite strong enrichment of Sir proteins at telomeric regions (Takahashi et al., 2011; Ellahi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Takahashi et al., 2011; Ellahi et al., 2015.

claim: Sir-based silencing is not a widespread phenomenon at telomeres despite strong enrichment of Sir proteins at telomeric regions.
source: However, this is consistent with the previous observation that expression of subtelomeric genes in S. cerevisiae is largely uninfluenced by mutations in Sir proteins and Sir-based silencing is not a widespread phenomenon at telomeres despite strong enrichment of Sir proteins at telomeric regions (Takahashi et al., 2011; Ellahi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Takahashi et al., 2011; Ellahi et al., 2015.

claim: SIR2 is not haploinsufficient for silencing.
source: However, this is unlikely because previous study (Dodson and Rine, 2015) and our own experiments showed that SIR2 is not haploinsufficient for silencing: heterozygous SIR2 diploid strain (Δsir2/SIR2), in which Sir2 level was reduced by an extent similar to that in disome X, did not compromise HML silencing (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Experimental data from heterozygous SIR2 diploid strain and citation to Dodson and Rine, 2015.

claim: Three genes (BNA1, BNA2, BNA4) involved in NAD biosynthesis pathway are located on Chr X.
source: Second, we explored the possibility that NAD biosynthesis could be compromised because three genes (BNA1, BNA2, BNA4) involved in this pathway are located on Chr X, and low NAD levels have been linked to defective silencing phenotypes (Grozinger et al., 2001; Sandmeier et al., 2002; Bedalov et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on genomic location information and known gene functions.

claim: Low NAD levels have been linked to defective silencing phenotypes.
source: Second, we explored the possibility that NAD biosynthesis could be compromised because three genes (BNA1, BNA2, BNA4) involved in this pathway are located on Chr X, and low NAD levels have been linked to defective silencing phenotypes (Grozinger et al., 2001; Sandmeier et al., 2002; Bedalov et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Grozinger et al., 2001; Sandmeier et al., 2002; Bedalov et al., 2003.

claim: Supplementing disome X strains with NAD did not rescue the desilencing phenotype.
source: However, supplementing disome X strains with NAD did not rescue the desilencing phenotype (data not shown).
evidence: Experimental test of NAD supplementation showed no rescue of desilencing.

claim: Aneuploidy confers complex or significant phenotypic changes by multigenic mechanisms.
source: This is consistent with previous studies showing that aneuploidy confers complex or significant phenotypic changes by multigenic mechanisms (Selmecki et al., 2006; Rancati et al., 2008; Selmecki et al., 2008; Pavelka et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2012, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Selmecki et al., 2006; Rancati et al., 2008; Selmecki et al., 2008; Pavelka et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2012, 2015.

claim: Heterochromatin-like regions are tethered to the nuclear periphery and form a specialized structural compartment, which is required for Sir proteins to establish silencing.
source: Another possible mechanism by which aneuploidy could impact silencing is by affecting the defined chromosome organization within the nucleus, whereby heterochromatin-like regions are tethered to the nuclear periphery and form a specialized structural compartment, which is required for Sir proteins to establish silencing (Andrulis et al., 1998; Mekhail et al., 2008; Bystricky et al., 2009; Ruault et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Andrulis et al., 1998; Mekhail et al., 2008; Bystricky et al., 2009; Ruault et al., 2011.
